text: Dadabhai Naoroji (4 September 1825 – 30 June 1917) was an Indian political leader, merchant, scholar, and writer who played a significant role in both Indian and British public life. He was a founding member of the Indian National Congress and served as its President from 1886 to 1887, 1893 to 1894, and 1906 to 1907. Naoroji began his career as the Diwan (Minister) of Baroda in 1874, under the patronage of Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III, and later became Prime Minister of Baroda in 1874. He was also a member of the Legislative Council of Bombay (1885–88) and the Indian National Association founded by Sir Surendranath Banerjea, which later merged into the Indian National Congress. Born in Navsari into a Gujarati-speaking Parsi Zoroastrian family, he was educated at the Elphinstone Institute School and became the first Indian to hold the position of Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy at Elphinstone College in Bombay in 1855. In 1855, he moved to London to become a partner in Cama & Co, opening a Liverpool branch, and later established his own cotton trading company, Dadabhai Naoroji & Co, in 1859. He also founded the Rahnumai Mazdayasan Sabha in 1851 and the Gujarati fortnightly publication Rast Goftar in 1854. In 1855, he launched The Voice of India. In 1865, he directed and launched the London Indian Society, and in 1867, he helped establish the East India Association, which aimed to present the Indian perspective to the British public and counter the Ethnological Society of London’s claims about Asian inferiority. The Association gained support from prominent Englishmen and influenced British parliamentary discourse, with branches in Mumbai, Kolkata, and Chennai. Naoroji moved to Britain again and was elected as a Liberal Party Member of Parliament for Finsbury Central in 1892, becoming the first British Indian MP; he refused to take the oath on the Bible, instead using his copy of the Khordeh Avesta, and was later invited to become Governor of the Imperial Institute. He was married to Gulbai at the age of 11 and died in Bombay on 30 June 1917 at the age of 91. He is best known for formulating the "drain theory," which argued that British colonial rule led to a transfer of wealth from India to Britain. In his 1901 publication Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, he estimated a drain of 200–300 million pounds from India’s revenue to Britain that was not recirculated into India. He identified six factors contributing to this drain, including the exploitation of Indian labor, unequal trade valuations, and the export of Indian goods using funds drained from India. He believed that while some tribute was necessary for services like railways, the profits from these services did not benefit India and instead enriched Britain. British workers were allowed to take home earnings from India, and the East India Company used drained funds to purchase Indian goods for export. Naoroji argued that allowing Indian professionals equal employment opportunities would reduce the drain and that India’s industries should grow to generate domestic revenue. He also emphasized the moral and material loss to India due to colonial rule and warned of despotism and destruction if Indians were denied a voice in governance. His work influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who wrote to him in 1894 expressing deep admiration, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who stated that if only one Indian representative were allowed in the British Parliament, it would be Naoroji. Naoroji was a member of the Second International and engaged with socialist networks alongside Karl Kautsky and Georgi Plekhanov, maintaining a moderate stance on political issues. His efforts contributed to the creation of the Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure in 1896, which reviewed financial burdens on India. He is regarded as one of the most important figures in the early Indian independence movement and is often remembered as the "Grand Old Man of Indian Nationalism." In recognition of his contributions, the British government introduced the Dadabhai Naoroji Awards in 2014, launched by Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg, and India Post issued commemorative stamps in 1963, 1997, and 2017. A plaque honoring him was unveiled by English Heritage in 2022 at his former home in Bromley, London, and a blue plaque is located outside the Finsbury Town Hall in London. Roads named after him include Dadabhai Naoroji Road in Mumbai, Karachi, and Naoroji Street in Finsbury, London, and a residential colony in Delhi is named Naoroji Nagar. His granddaughters, Perin and Khurshedben, were involved in the independence movement, with Khurshedben arrested in 1930 for attempting to hoist the Indian flag in Ahmedabad. Naoroji’s legacy continues to be studied in the context of Indian nationalism, colonial critique, and early Asian participation in British politics.
